description: Indigenous people of northern Japan, Sakhalin, and the Kuril Islands whose Ainu language, bear ceremonialism, and salmon-fishing culture were distinct from mainland Japanese civilisation; the Ainu inhabited Hokkaido and adjacent islands as hunter-gatherers and traders of furs and seafood integrated into Japanese, Chinese, and later Russian commercial networks before Meiji-era colonisation suppressed their cultural autonomy.

geographic.no_central_capital_reason: Decentralised hunter-gatherer society; no fixed capital.

lifecycle_phases.description: Ainu ancestors inhabited Hokkaido and parts of Honshu; semi-nomadic hunter-gatherer economy based on salmon, deer, and bear.
Distinctive Ainu culture crystallised with elaborate bear ceremonies, oral tradition (yukar epics), and extensive trade with mainland Japan and the continent.
Japanese expansion northward from Honshu compressed Ainu territory; conflict with Wajin settlers increased and trading relationships became more asymmetric.

rise_factors.description: Dense forests and island geography of Hokkaido shielded Ainu communities from full conquest.
Rich salmon runs and marine resources supported dense populations relative to climate.
Shared animist cosmology and bear-ceremony ritual cycle bound dispersed communities.

decline_factors.description: Sustained Wajin colonisation from southern Honshu progressively displaced Ainu from productive coastal lowlands.
Incorporation into Japanese trade networks eroded Ainu economic autonomy.
Epidemic disease introduced via expanding contact with Japanese merchants reduced population.
